the structure of the Fab fragment from a monoclonal anti-HPr antibody was solved by the molecular replacement method, and the structure of the antigen-binding site of this antibody was determined.

the elucidation of the molecular basis for antigen recognition.
the structure of the antibody-antigen complex, the nature of the antigenic determinants, and the molecular basis of the antigen-antibody reaction.
the elucidation of the structural basis for the recognition of a small phosphocarrying protein, HPr, by a monoclonal immunoglobulin, Jel 42.

the Fab Jel 41 molecule is structurally similar to Fab HED 1O but has some differences which are due to the differences in amino acid sequences of their variable regions and/or their different antigenic specificities.
the Fab Jel 12 structure has been determined and that the structure of this antibody is very similar to that of other Fab fragments.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Fab Jel 41 has the same general structure as Fab HED 12, but that there are significant differences between the hypervarible loops which account for its different antigen specificity.

the structure determination of Fab Jel42 has provided a new example of the use of the search model method of solving crystal structures and has shown that the search model method can be used to determine the structure of a Fab fragment even when the Fab molecule has a large elbow angle and no local noncrystalline axis of symmetry.
the structure of a Fab fragment with a high affinity for a protein antigen can be solved using a Fab fragment with low affinity for the antigen as a search model.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is feasible to determine the three-dimensional structure of a monoclonally derived Fab fragment using molecular replacement.
the elbow angle is not a good indicator of the relative orientation of the variable domains.
the elbow angle of the Fab molecule is a highly conserved feature, and that this is true despite the presence of a large number of hypervariable residues in the antigen-binding region.
